concepts.def: A value showing the degree of oxidation of an atom.
Tendency of a half-cell to gain electrons, measured against hydrogen.
Two half-cells producing an EMF from a redox reaction.
Using electricity to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction.
Show what happens at each electrode.

walkthroughs.body_html:
More positive E° -> reduction at cathode. More negative E° -> oxidation at anode.

E°cell = E°(cathode) - E°(anode). Always positive for a spontaneous cell.

Convention: oxidised | reduced || reduced | oxidised, with anode left and cathode right.

Example: Zn(s) | Zn^2+ || Cu^2+ | Cu(s). Single bar = phase boundary, double = salt bridge.

Non-standard conditions shift E from E° (Nernst, qualitative). Increasing [oxidised] makes E more positive.

For Cu^2+/Cu electrode, raising [Cu^2+] pushes reduction equilibrium right, E becomes more positive.

mcqs.q: In a standard hydrogen electrode used as a reference, what is the assigned electrode potential?
options: Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
The standard hydrogen electrode actually has zero potential because hydrogen has no charge.
Exactly 0 V by convention — all other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.

mcqs.q: Can a single standard electrode potential be measured in isolation?
options: The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
No — electrode potentials are RELATIVE values measured against a reference (the standard hydrogen electrode, defined as 0 V).
Each electrode has an absolute potential that can be measured directly with a voltmeter.

mcqs.q: If E°cell for a redox reaction is positive, what does that tell you?
options: Standard electrode potentials are measured by submerging the electrode in pure water.
A positive E°cell means the reaction is exothermic in every case.
A positive E°cell guarantees the reaction will happen rapidly at room temperature.
The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — but it may still be very slow if kinetic barriers are high.
